## Phenomenon

A nonlinear action of the additive group $\mathbb G_a$ on $\mathbb A^7$ has a non-finitely generated ring of invariants [@roberts1990]. In contrast to [Nagata's counterexample](../nagata/index.qmd), the group is one-dimensional and the action is not linear.

## Setup

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero and set
$$
B=k[x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2,y_3,z].
$$
For $t\in\mathbb G_a$, define
$$
\begin{aligned}
t\cdot(x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2,y_3,z)
=\bigl(&x_1,x_2,x_3,\\
&y_1+tx_1^3,\ y_2+tx_2^3,\ y_3+tx_3^3,\\
&z+t(x_1x_2x_3)^2\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$
Because the $x_i$ remain fixed, composing two such transformations adds their parameters. Thus this formula defines an algebraic group action.

Its corresponding derivation is
$$
D=x_1^3\frac{\partial}{\partial y_1}
 +x_2^3\frac{\partial}{\partial y_2}
 +x_3^3\frac{\partial}{\partial y_3}
 +(x_1x_2x_3)^2\frac{\partial}{\partial z}.
$$
It lowers total degree in $y_1,y_2,y_3,z$, so it is locally nilpotent: every polynomial is killed by some iterate of $D$. In characteristic zero, invariance is equivalent to being killed by this derivation. Roberts' theorem states that
$$
A:=B^{\mathbb G_a}=\ker D
\quad\text{is not finitely generated over }k.
$$
See @roberts1990 for the original construction and @dufresne2015 [§9] for this formulation.

Geometrically, the action translates each fibre of the projection to the three $x$-coordinates in a direction depending polynomially on the base point. Away from the origin of that base, the direction is nonzero. Over the origin, the whole fibre is fixed: the fixed-point locus is the affine four-space defined by $x_1=x_2=x_3=0$.

## Construction

The following polynomials are invariant:
$$
x_i,\qquad
u_{ij}=x_i^3y_j-x_j^3y_i,\qquad
b_i=x_i z-x_j^2x_k^2y_i,
$$
where $\{i,j,k\}=\{1,2,3\}$ in the last expression. In each case, applying $D$ produces two terms that cancel.

The proof below uses Roberts' existence lemma [@roberts1990, Lemma 3; @freudenburg2001, §3.3]: for every $n\geq0$, there is an invariant
$$
\beta_n=x_1z^n+\text{terms of lower }z\text{-degree}.
$$
The lemma is used without proof.

## Proof of non-finite generation

Set $I=(x_1,x_2,x_3)B$. First, every invariant is constant modulo $I$. To see this, take $f\in A$ and write its part of total $x$-degree zero as $f_0(y_1,y_2,y_3,z)$. The part of $Df=0$ of $x$-degree three gives
$$
\sum_{i=1}^3x_i^3\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial y_i}=0.
$$
Hence $f_0$ is independent of the $y_i$. Next compare the coefficient of $x_1^2x_2^2x_3^2$ in $Df$. Contributions from the $y_i$-derivatives are divisible by some $x_i^3$, so this coefficient is precisely $\partial f_0/\partial z$. It also vanishes, and characteristic zero implies $f_0\in k$.

Now suppose $A$ had finitely many algebra generators. Subtracting their constants gives generators $g_1,\ldots,g_r\in I$. Modulo $I^2$, every polynomial in these generators is a constant plus a linear combination of their images: all products of two generators vanish.

Consequently, the image of $A$ in $B/I^2$ would be finite-dimensional over $k$. But the images of the $\beta_n$ are linearly independent. In any finite relation, the term with largest index has a unique highest power of $z$, with nonzero coefficient $x_1$ modulo $I^2$. This is a contradiction.

The argument shows that the $\beta_n$ remain linearly independent modulo $I^2$, where products of invariants lying in $I$ vanish.

## Outro

In characteristic zero, Weitzenböck's theorem gives finite generation for every linear $\mathbb G_a$-action [@freudenburg2001, §1]. Roberts' example therefore cannot be made linear by a polynomial change of coordinates.

## References and related examples

Roberts published the example in 1990; it arose from his work on symbolic blow-ups [@roberts1990; @freudenburg2001, §3.1]. The additive-group interpretation was recognised independently by A'Campo-Neuen and by Deveney and Finston [@acampo1994; @deveney1994; @freudenburg2001, §3.1]. A'Campo-Neuen also used Roberts' example to obtain a linear action of $\mathbb G_a^{12}$ on $\mathbb A^{19}$ with a non-finitely generated invariant ring [@acampo1994; @freudenburg2001, §2.2].

Kojima and Miyanishi gave a family of counterexamples in higher odd dimensions: for each $n\geq3$ and $t\geq2$, the derivation of $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_n,z]$ with $D(x_i)=0$, $D(y_i)=x_i^{t+1}$ and $D(z)=(x_1\cdots x_n)^t$ has a non-finitely generated kernel [@kojima1997; @freudenburg2001, §3.2].

Freudenburg's survey [@freudenburg2001] describes the history of these examples, and Dufresne and Kraft discuss the action in @dufresne2015 [§9].
